<action type="say">
First priority is preventing leaks and damage, then safely thawing the pipe.

A few quick questions so I can be specific:
1) Where are you located (city/region and house/apartment)?
2) Is any part of that pipe visible under the sink, and is it metal (copper/steel) or plastic (PVC/PEX)?
3) Do you see any bulging, cracks, or dripping around the pipes or fittings under the sink right now?
4) When you turn on the kitchen faucet:
   - No water at all from hot/cold?
   - Or reduced flow?
5) Do other faucets in the house work normally?

For now, do this immediately:
- DON’T use an open flame (propane torch, lighter, etc.) on the pipe.
- If you can, turn off the water just to that sink (small shutoff valves under the sink). Turn both hot and cold to the OFF position (right/clockwise).
- Leave the faucet handle in the ON/OPEN position (both hot and cold) so if it thaws, pressure can escape as a trickle instead of bursting the pipe.

Tell me your answers to those questions and what you see under the sink, and I’ll give you step‑by‑step thawing instructions tailored to your setup and let you know if you should call someone out tonight or can likely handle it yourself. </action>

<action type="say">
This sounds like a localized freeze on the kitchen run, with main supply still fine. Goal: gently warm that section and nearby wall/cabinet, and be ready in case a hidden section has cracked.

First, quick safety setup (2–3 minutes):
1) Put a bucket or large bowl under the visible pipes and where they meet the wall/cabinet.
2) Clear everything out of the cabinet so air/heat can get in.
3) Leave the kitchen faucet ON (both hot and cold handles).

Now, gentle thawing steps you can try:

Option A – Hair dryer (best if you have one)
1) Set to low or medium heat.
2) Start at the faucet supply lines under the sink (the metal pipes/hoses going up to the faucet), then work back toward where the pipes disappear into the wall or cabinet.
3) Keep the dryer moving, 4–6 inches away—don’t concentrate in one spot.
4) Do this for 10–15 minutes, pausing every few minutes to feel if any part of the pipe is warming slightly.

Option B – Space heater (if you have a small, safe one)
1) Place it outside the cabinet, blowing warm air into the open under-sink area.
2) Keep it at least a foot away from anything and don’t leave it unattended.
3) Let it run 20–30 minutes, checking the pipes periodically with your hand (should feel cool → less cool over time, not hot).

Option C – Warm towels
1) Soak towels in warm (not boiling) water and wring them out well.
2) Wrap around the visible metal sections under the sink, especially near where they enter the wall/cabinet.
3) Swap/re-warm every 10–15 minutes.

While you’re doing any of these:
- Watch the faucet: if you hear gurgling or see a trickle, that’s good—let it run.
- Watch under the sink and around the wall penetration: if you see dripping, spraying, or sudden wet spots, turn OFF the shutoff valves under the sink immediately (clockwise) and then turn the faucet OFF.

Because you’re in a high-rise:
- If you have a building maintenance/super/concierge number, it’s worth calling them now to let them know a kitchen line is frozen. They may already know of a colder line in your stack and can advise or send someone.
- If at any point:
  • You can’t get water back after 30–40 minutes of gentle warming, or  
  • You see any leaks, or hear water behind the wall,  
  stop and get building maintenance involved. They know the building’s shutoff locations and liability situation.

Two clarifiers so I can fine-tune:
1) Do the pipes under the sink disappear straight into an outside wall, or is it an interior wall/cabinet (e.g., island, wall shared with another unit/hall)?
2) Do you have a hair dryer or a small space heater available?

Tell me what you have on hand and what kind of wall this is, and I’ll adjust the next steps—and if you want, I can also walk you through what exactly to say when you call building maintenance so they take it seriously but don’t panic. </action>

<action type="say">
Since it’s an exterior wall and you’ve got a hair dryer, that’s our main tool. The risk spot is usually where the pipe passes through or runs along that cold exterior wall.

Step-by-step with the hair dryer (about 20–30 min total):
1) Prep
   - Keep the kitchen faucet ON (both hot and cold).
   - Bucket/bowl under the pipes and where they enter the wall.
   - Cabinet doors under the sink open to let room air in.

2) Warm the visible pipes first
   - Set the dryer to medium heat.
   - Start where the flexible lines or rigid pipes go up to the faucet, then move down toward the shutoff valves, then toward the wall.
   - Keep the dryer moving, 4–6 inches away. Don’t focus on one point for more than a few seconds.

3) Focus near the wall
   - Spend extra time gently warming the area where the pipes disappear into the exterior wall or along that wall section inside the cabinet.
   - If the wall feels very cold, you can slowly move the dryer back and forth over the wall surface right around the pipe entry.

4) While you’re heating:
   - Listen for gurgling or air in the line and watch the faucet—first sign of success is usually a little sputter or trickle. Let it run; don’t shut it off.
   - Keep checking under the sink and around the wall opening for any beads of water, drips, or spraying.
   - If you see ANY leak: 
     • Turn both shutoff valves under the sink OFF (clockwise).  
     • Then turn the faucet OFF.  
     • Take a quick photo of the area and call building maintenance right away to report a suspected burst or pinhole leak in the exterior-wall line.

Timing / when to escalate:
- If you’ve done 20–30 minutes of careful warming and absolutely nothing changes at the faucet:
  • Stop, and call building maintenance.  
  • Tell them: “Kitchen supply line appears frozen in the exterior wall. Bathroom fixtures have normal water. No visible leaks yet, but hair-dryer warming at cabinet hasn’t restored flow.”

- If water comes back:
  • Let it run at a trickle for a while (10–15 min) to flush and keep water moving.
  • Feel around the wall area and cabinet floor for dampness just in case a small split only opens under pressure.

Because you’re in a high-rise, building maintenance is your first call before an outside plumber—they control the building-side shutoffs and may want to inspect that stack.

If you’d like, do one round of the hair-dryer warming, then tell me:
- Did you get any sputter/trickle at the faucet?
- Any dampness or dripping under the sink or along the wall?

Based on that, I’ll help you decide if it’s safe to keep using it, keep thawing, or if it’s time to get maintenance/a plumber lined up. </action>

<action type="say">
At this point it’s likely the freeze is deeper in the wall or farther along the kitchen run where you can’t safely reach it, so continuing with the dryer isn’t going to help much and could dry out the area unnecessarily.

Next step: loop in building maintenance

Call or message building maintenance and say something like:
- “My kitchen sink supply line appears to be frozen in the exterior wall. I have zero flow from both hot and cold at the kitchen faucet, but bathroom fixtures and toilet work normally. I warmed the exposed pipes under the sink with a hair dryer for about 25 minutes; there are no visible leaks or damp spots under the sink. It seems like the freeze is in the wall or building line. Can someone check this stack and the kitchen line, and advise on next steps?”

While you’re waiting:
1) Leave the under-sink shutoff valves OPEN and the faucet handles in the ON position for now.  
   - If they thaw it from the building side, you’ll see flow start or hear it—and you’re already in position to spot a leak quickly.
2) Keep the bucket/bowl and cabinet clear.
3) Check under the sink every so often for any sudden dampness or dripping.

If maintenance tells you they can’t do much or it’ll be a long delay and you want to bring in a plumber yourself:
- I can help you find and schedule an emergency plumber in Minneapolis.  
  - Tell me: your building’s approximate neighborhood/ZIP, how urgent you want this (right away vs later today), and whether you care more about cost or speed.

Otherwise, once you’ve spoken with maintenance, let me know what they say and I can help you interpret their plan, what to watch for, and what to push for if needed. </action>
